units.la: CUm haec P. Rami Basilea Basileæ scripta forté in nostras manus incidisset, eam maluimus illo inscio prælo committi, quæ adferret tibi nihil adiumenti, quam veluti sepultam in tenebris delitescere. Quam-obrem nostrum hoc in te studium & operam boni consulite.
units.tr: When this Basilea by P. Ramus, written at Basel, happened by chance to fall into our hands, we preferred to have it printed without his knowledge, since it would bring you no benefit if it lay hidden in darkness, as if buried. Therefore, kindly accept this zeal and effort of ours on your behalf.

units.la: PETRI RAMI BASILEA AD SENATUM POPULUM QUE BASILIENSEM.
units.tr: Basilea: To the Senate and People of Basel, by Peter Ramus.

units.la: MEMINI (viri Basilienses) semperque dum vi-vam meminero, quam jucunda, quam libera-lis, quam humana Basilensis habitatio nobis accciderit. Etenim pleraque egregia de civita-te & academia Basilensi absens audieram: at præsens majora atque ampliora omnia expertus sum. Urbs in Rauracorum agro frumenti, vini, frugumque omnium feracissimo per intermedium Rhenum veterem Galliæ Germaniæque terminum duobus velut oppidis altero Gallico altero Germanico apte, & ad fluminis commodi-tates opportune dividitur. A Gallia vallis rivo Birsula deprimitur, à meridie angustior, in septetrionem ad flu-vium usque latior, eaque, cum gemino utrinque jugo partem civitatis ædificiorum civiumque frequentia præ-cipuam complectitur. Gallica Basilea hæc major est, quæ Rheni sui velut amore capta secundum ipsius ripam é dorso montis excisam latius extenditur: a Germania pla-nicies est modice in flumen declivis, ambitu rotundior, lateribusque ideo contractior: Germanica Basilea hæc minor est. Itaque Rhenus ponte partim lapideo, partim sublicio jūctus, é duabus urbibus unam efficit: unde Ba-silea quasi Passilia á passu (qui Gallis trajectus est) Beato Rhenano videtur appellata. Satis vero constat augustam Rauracorum á L. Munatio Planco Romanam fuisse coloniam, cujus hodicque ruinæ sepulchrum permagnæ urbis oftedunt. Et verisimile est, etiam florente augusta trajectum eundem fuisse propter humiliorem ripam, ideoque cum Germanis comerciorum usum faciliorem. Marcellinus Basiliam nominat, eique vicinum castellum Roboris nomine tacita interim Augusta: ut jam tū quo- que Augusta deleta fuisse videatur, & ejus ruinis Basilea excrevisse. Sed Basilii etiam Sarmatæ ad utramque Danubii ripam apud Strabonem sunt, qui utrum huc aliqua belli tempestate deducti, nomen urbi dederint conjici- endum relinquo. Certe Basilea nostra longe prudentiores, quam Augusta illa conditores habuit. Quemadmodum enim Laconibus Apollo respondit Byzantium é regione cæcorum collocādum, Chalcedonios cæcos significans, qui præterito opportuniore ad Europam litore asiaticum litus urbi suæ delegissent: sic Romanos in deducenda colonia asperitates saxorum & montium seculos præ nostris Basiliis longe pręstatiorem regionem legentibus, cæcos dixeris fuisse. Sed a quocumque Basilea vel constructa vel appellata sit, duo præterea fluvioli Rheno adjuncti, Viesa ex Hercynia sylva, Birsa ex jura monte nō solum permagnam piscium & lignorum copiam, sed varios generum omnium commeatus Basileam convehunt: adeoque Birsa chartaceis & frumentariis, Viesa etiam ferratoriis armorumque cudendorum ac poliendorum mirificis molis & machinis, plurimorū artificum manus operasque longissime superant. Aquæ vero præter Rhenum, Viesam, Birsam, Birsulam saluberrimæ per totam tam urbem derivatur: vt fontibus tum publicis tum privatis supra trecentos perennibus, civitas non modo ad quotidianum civium usum potando, lavando, aquando, subitis incendiorum casibus occurrendo, sed imprimis ad insigne decus urbis & ornamentum prędita sit. Vię ut per interclusam vallem aut juga montium licuit, amplis regionibus directæ sunt, aut per clivos arduos & præcipites non modo gradibus insinuatę, sed ligneis utrinque fulciis, quibus aut descensus lapsum cohibeas, aut ascensus laborem subleves, instructæ: ædificia vero compluribus contignationibus eleganti, atque imprimis optica pictură varietate decorantur: Quę omnia sunt ante oculos: Sub terra vero structurę fornicum ac testudinum, ad munditiem urbis corradendis undique & abluendis sordibus, per vrbem totam plurimę Birsulam accipiunt: qui interdum (ut anno 1528) inundatione sua urbis vallem pene obruit: ideoque licet exiguus attamen amplis & variis ductibus dividitur, singulisque hebdomadis per val-lis vias ad pavimentum converrendum expurgandúque deducitur: & tamen subterraneæ machinationes istæ urbem quondam anno 1356 ingenti terræ motu cum sexaginta vicinis arcibus afflictam proflratamque videntur etiam a tali calamitate impostrum liberiorem reddidisse. Itaque hoc unum meo quidem judicio præcipue suspiciendum est, præcipueque celebrandum. Etenim ex operibꝰ urbis Romę Plinius cloacas á Tarquinio factas, & ab Agrippa restitutas suffossis montibus septemque corrivatis amnibus, ad rapiedum auferenduque omnia coactis ita celebrat ut nullum neque majus neque mira-bilius arbitretur. Ergo Basilea tanquam illa pensilis & sub-ternavigabilis Roma cloacis expurgatur & abluitur: aë-risque amoenitas licet ex ipsa quidem caeli clementia lo-co naturalis, operibus tamen istis adjuta, cum pari & a-grorum fertilitate & aquarum salubritate ita consensisse videtur & conspirasse, ut quacunque urbis porta egredi iubeat, thessalica tempe vel frugum varietate vel prato-rum arborumque viriditate, vel inaequabili montium valliumque dissimilitudine protinus appareat. Sed tem-pe ne extra civitatem cives curiosius exquirerent, tria sunt ipsis in media urbe constituta: Prima sunt ad Rhe-num ponte maximo & latissimo conjunctum, & cum quolibet orbis fluvio delectatione & voluptate compa-randum. Cydnus mediam Tharsum interfluit, liquore tanto, tantaque riparum suavitate, ut Alexandrum tam singularis aspectus gratia captum invitarit ad regiu[?] cor-pus pulvere sudoreque abluendum: Sed gelidus fluminis rigor regem pene interemit, Rhenus est ille quidè perinde aspectabilis, sed innoxius, praecipitemque é ponte juventutem benigne excipit, natantemque recreat ac re-ficit. Itaque aestivo imprimis vespertinoque tempore ci-ves aut inambulantes, aut ad claustra pontis innixos ita jucundus latissimi rapidissimique fluminis aspectus & le-niter aspiras aura delectat, ut Tharsenses Basileam ve-nerint Cydnum suum pro Rheno facile despiciant. Alte-ra tempe sunt ad marianum templum, alta & sublimi rupe cum sua natura tum lapide quadrato contra Rheni minas impetusque validissime communita. Hic agger tiliam habet, patulis ramis artificiose digestis imprimis opacam, umbraque propterea perjucundam: despectus est deinde longe dextra sinistraque tanquam in clarissimum speculum, sic in subjectum Rhenum: ante sunt colles varii, duo circiter millia passuum vitibus & sylvis ve-stiti atque ornati, ut opticam oculis gratiorem videre me non meminerim. Sed delicias meas Sampetreum viridarium aut potius Martis lucum, nisi tempe longe suavissima dixero, indignus ejus suavitate merito existimer. Spa-tium est velut in pomerio intra veteris novaeque urbis moenia comprehensum: a meridie armamentaria tanquam Martis quoddam templum, specie sua magnificum objectum est: ab occasu & ortu martiae palestrae duae sunt, illic virorum, hic juvenum, ubi festis diebus balistarii exercetur: ad septentrionem privatorum civium sunt horti. Campus martis ita conclusus a vehiculorum & pecorum molestiis liber. Liberali civium oblectationi con-secratus jugera circiter quatuor in quadrum, tiliis & ulmis centum & quadraginta ita distinguitur, ut tres am-bulationes intermedi spatiis fere aequalibus pedes circiter quadraginta dividantur: extrema & viis & arboribus confusiora sunt. Diagonius quadrati ad geminos aditus oppositos ab ęde [?] facto Petro sacra, & a porta Spalea duos fontes habet, alterum quod praecipuum viridarii specta-culum est, annosae quercus veluti nutricium: Hæc martia quercus tiliam illam vincit amplitudine: brachia é trunco septem pedes alto circumquaque decem primaria defledeflectitur, singulaque in alia deinceps bina, terna, qua-terna etiā quædam dissecta ramis per totam caveam infinitis expanduntur: columnæ ligneæ triplici ordine faciunt figuram primo sexangulam, deinde nonangulam, postremo sedecangulam. Enimvero celebrata est platanus in lycia, gelidi fontis socia[?] amœnitate itineri opposita, domicilii modo cava L x x x. atque unius pedum spe-cu, nemoroso vertice, & se vastis protegens ramis arborum instar, agros longis obtinens umbris: ac ne quid desit speluncæ imagini, saxa intus crepidinis corona muscosos complexa punices: tam digna miraculo, ut Ficinius Mutianus ter Cons. & nuper provinciæ ejus legatus, prodendum etiam posteris putarit, epulatum intra eam se cum duodevicesimo comite, large ipsa thoros præbente fronde, ab omni afflatu securum, optantem imbrium per folia crepitus, lætiorem quam marmorum nitore, pi-cturæ varietate, laquearium auro, cubuisse in eadem. Atqui martia quercus fontis amœnitate vel umbræ opacitate cosimili, etiam imperatorem hospitem & convivam meruit: Literis enim proditum est imperatorem Frederi-cum cum filio Maximiliano anno 1474, umbra nostræ quercus tam patulis diffusę ramis delectatum, sub ea cum toto imperiali comitatu cœnavisse: ut quanto major est imperator consule, tanto sampetrea quercus lycia platano gloriosior habeatur. Itaque Martis Lucus omnibus civibus communis est, sed præcipue doctis & literatis dicatus. Dic igitur P. Virgili, dic carminibus tuis laudes viridarii nostri
units.tr: I remember, men of Basel, and I shall always remember as long as I live, how pleasant, how generous and how kindly our residence in Basel proved to be. I had heard many excellent things about the city and the university of Basel while I was away, but once I was present I found that everything exceeded and surpassed what I had heard. The city lies in the land of the Rauraci, most fertile in grain, wine and every kind of produce. The Rhine, the old boundary between Gaul and Germany, runs through it and divides it into two towns, as it were, one on the Gallic side and one on the German side, suitably placed and conveniently situated for the river's advantages. From the Gallic side a valley, cut by the stream Birsula, runs down. It is narrower at the south and wider toward the north, where it reaches the river, and between the twin ridges on either side it takes in the main part of the city's buildings and its crowded population. This Gallic Basel is the larger; it is as if it had been captivated by love of its Rhine, and it spreads more widely along the bank, cut out of the flank of the mountain. On the German side the ground is a level plain, gently sloping down to the river, rounder in its circuit and for that reason narrower in its sides; this German Basel is the smaller. So the Rhine, joined by a bridge partly of stone and partly of timber, makes one city out of two. Hence Beatus Rhenanus thinks Basel was named as if it were "Passilia," from the crossing (passus), which is what the Gauls called the ford. It is quite certain that the famous Rauraci town was made a Roman colony by Lucius Munatius Plancus, and its ruins to this day show the tomb of a very great city. It is also likely that, even while Augusta flourished, the same crossing existed because of the lower bank, and therefore trade with the Germans was easier. Marcellinus names Basilia, and next to it a small fortress called Robur, while Augusta is passed over in silence; so it seems that Augusta had by then been destroyed, and Basel grew up out of its ruins. But in Strabo there are also Basilii, Sarmatians, on both banks of the Danube; whether they were brought here by some storm of war and gave their name to the town, I leave for conjecture. Certainly our Basel had founders far wiser than those of that Augusta. For just as Apollo answered the Laconians that Byzantium should be founded opposite the land of the blind, meaning the Chalcedonians, who, passing by the more convenient shore facing Europe, had chosen the Asian shore for their city, so you might say the Romans, in founding their colony, were blind, since they chose the rough rocks and mountains rather than a region far better than our Basel. Yet from whatever source Basel was either built or named, two small streams joined to the Rhine, the Wiese from the Hercynian forest and the Birs from the Jura mountain, bring to Basel not only a very great abundance of fish and timber but every kind of supply, and the Birs far surpasses the hands and labour of many craftsmen in paper and grain, while the Wiese does so in iron-work and the wonderful machines and devices for forging and polishing arms. Moreover, besides the Rhine, the Wiese, the Birs and the Birsula, most wholesome water is channelled through the whole city, so that the town is provided with more than three hundred perennial fountains, both public and private, not only for the daily use of the citizens in drinking, washing and watering, and for meeting sudden fires, but above all as a remarkable adornment and ornament of the city. Roads, wherever the enclosed valley or the mountain ridges allowed, have been laid out through wide districts, or, where the slopes were steep and precipitous, have been cut into steps and fitted out on both sides with wooden supports, by which a descent can be checked from slipping or an ascent made less toilsome. The buildings are decorated with several storeys in an elegant manner and, above all, with a variety of painted work. All these things lie open to the eye. Beneath the ground, however, there are structures of vaults and arches, through which the Birsula flows into very many parts of the city to sweep and wash away the filth from every side and keep the town clean. Sometimes, as in the year 1528, it has flooded and nearly overwhelmed the valley of the city. Therefore, although it is small, it is divided by many wide and varied channels, and every week it is led through the streets of the valley to sweep and cleanse the pavement. And yet those underground works seem to have made the city, which in the year 1356 was struck and laid low by a great earthquake along with sixty neighbouring fortresses, freer from such a calamity in future. So this one thing, in my judgment, deserves above all to be admired and above all to be celebrated. For among the works of the city of Rome, Pliny celebrates the sewers made by Tarquin and restored by Agrippa, with mountains dug through and seven rivers diverted and gathered together to carry off and remove everything, in such a way that he thinks nothing greater or more marvellous. Thus Basel, like that Rome hanging high and navigable underneath, is cleansed and washed by its sewers; and the pleasantness of the air, though natural to the place from the very mildness of the sky, is aided by these works, and it seems to agree and combine with the equal fertility of the fields and the healthfulness of the waters, so that whichever gate of the city you bid them go out by, there at once appears either a Vale of Tempe, by the variety of crops, the greenness of meadows and trees, or the uneven and unlike shapes of mountains and valleys. But so that the citizens might not look too curiously for pleasant places outside the city, there are three of them set up in the middle of the town. The first is by the Rhine, joined to the great and very wide bridge, and it is to be compared in delight and pleasure with any river in the world. The Cydnus flows through the middle of Tarsus, with such a flood and such a sweetness of banks that it invited Alexander, captivated by its singular beauty, to bathe his royal body of dust and sweat; but the cold chill of the stream almost killed the king. The Rhine is indeed equally pleasing to look at, but harmless, and it kindly receives the youth who leap from the bridge and refreshes and restores them as they swim. So especially in summer and in the evening, the citizens, either strolling about or leaning on the bridge's railings, are delighted by the view of this widest and swiftest river and by the gentle breathing breeze, so that men of Tarsus who came to Basel would easily look down upon their own Cydnus in comparison with the Rhine. The second place is the Vale of Tempe by the Marian temple, fortified most strongly against the threats and onslaughts of the Rhine on a high and lofty rock, both by its natural site and by squared stone. Here the embankment has linden trees, with their spreading branches skilfully arranged, very shady and therefore most pleasant in the shade. From it there is a long view to the right and left, as into a most bright mirror, and so down onto the Rhine beneath; in front are various hills, about two thousand paces off, clothed and adorned with vines and woods, so that I cannot remember seeing a prospect more pleasing to the eyes. But my delight, the St Peter's pleasure-ground, or rather the grove of Mars, would deserve to be thought unworthy of its sweetness if I did not call it by far the most charming of all. The space is enclosed, as it were on the pomerium, within the walls of the old and new town. On the south side there lies, magnificent in its appearance, the arsenal, like a kind of temple of Mars; on the west and east there are two Martial wrestling-grounds, one for men and one for young men, where the crossbowmen practise on feast days; on the north there are the gardens of private citizens. The Campus Martius, thus enclosed, is kept free from the nuisance of carriages and cattle. Dedicated to the free recreation of the citizens, it covers about four acres square and is divided by a hundred and forty lindens and elms, so that three walks, at roughly equal intervals, are separated by spaces of about forty feet; the outer parts are more confused, both with paths and with trees. The diagonals of the square, opposite each other, have two springs, one at the two opposite entrances, from the church dedicated to St Peter and from the Spalen gate. The chief sight of the pleasure-ground is an ancient oak, as it were the nurse of the whole place. This Martial oak surpasses that linden in size. From its trunk, seven feet high, ten main branches bend out on every side, and each of these in turn divides into two, three or even four, and some are split into innumerable branches spreading through the whole enclosure. Its wooden columns form, in three ranks, a figure first six-sided, then nine-sided, and lastly sixteen-sided. Indeed the plane tree in Lycia is celebrated, placed beside the road for the pleasantness of a cold spring, with a hollow like a dwelling, sixty paces round and a single hole in the top, wooded at the crown, sheltering itself with vast branches like a tree, and holding the fields in long shadows. And so that nothing should be lacking to the likeness of a cave, rocks inside, wrapped in a mossy crown of ledges, complete it. It was so worthy of wonder that Ficinius Mutianus, thrice consul and lately legate of that province, thought it should be handed down to posterity that he feasted within it with an eighteen-man retinue, the foliage itself providing couches generously, safe from every breeze, and that he lay down in it, delighted, wishing for the patter of rain on the leaves more than the gleam of marble, the variety of paintings or the gold of panelled ceilings. And yet the Martial oak has earned, by the pleasantness of its spring and the density of its shade, a similar honour: an emperor as guest and dinner companion. For it is recorded in writing that the Emperor Frederick, with his son Maximilian in the year 1474, delighted by the shade of our oak spread out with such wide branches, dined beneath it with his whole imperial retinue. So, just as the emperor is greater than a consul, so the St Peter's oak is held more glorious than the Lycian plane. Thus the Grove of Mars is common to all the citizens, but it is dedicated above all to the learned and the men of letters. Tell me, then, Publius Virgil, tell in your verses the praises of our pleasure-ground.

units.la: Hic interflumina nota Et fontes sacros frigus captabis opacum. Dic vero & caussam opaci frigoris Tum fylvis scena coruscis Desuper horrentique atrum nenus imminet umbra, Nympharum domus. O Poëtam elegantem & festivum viridarii nostri praeconem, Concludito igitur praeconium etiam elegantiore carmine ac festiviore Hic tibi Grynaei nemoris dicatur origo, Ne quis sit lucus, quo plus se jactet Apollo. Quapropter charitum tam variarum gratia, Nota magis nulli domus est sua, quam mihi lucus Martis.
units.tr: Here you will find the well-known streams and holy springs and seek cool shade. Tell also the cause of the shady coolness: the stage glitters with woods, and above it the dark grove looms with its bristling shade, the home of the Nymphs. O elegant poet and cheerful herald of our grove! Let him then conclude his praise in a more elegant and more cheerful song: here let the origin of the Grynean grove be told to you, lest any grove boast more than Apollo does. Therefore, through the charm of the Graces so varied, no house is more familiar to anyone than the grove of Mars is to me.

units.la: Vt id Poëta quoque ille de suo nobis gratificetur.Per-mittite itaque mihi(viri Basilienses)ut desideria votaque nostrarum in hoc luco inambulationum vobis simpliciter aperiam. Habet Academia Parisiensis pratum clericorum, velut item campum martium: pro quo adversus miserabilem studiosorum calamitatem legatus ad Hen-ricum Regem ea cum meis collegis sum consequutus, quae legationis illius oratione describuntur. Itaque nequaquam honestissimae civitati suos elysios invideo, sed academiae Parisiensi consimiles vehementer exopto. Verum in mearum delitiarum commemoratione diutius haereo: sit Basilea urbs elegantissima uberrimaque. Propterea-que concilium Basiliense ab anno 1473 ad annum 1490 retinuerit, elegantiores tamen & pulchriores sunt urbis mores:Etenim ista omnia & á natura & ab hominum arte atque industria peregrinis jucundissima sunt atque gratissima, quanto jucundiora atque gratiora illa ar-bitramur esse, cum evangelica religione ac pietate ita moratam civitatem perspiciunt, ut in ea iuste atque integre viuentibus nihil pręter Deum sanctasque leges verendum sit? Arca auri atque argenti plena vel incustoditis foribus aperta sit, furtum nullum formidatur: Virgo sit forma quamlibet eleganti atque eximia, raptoris nulla violetia metuitur: inermis vel intempesta nocte in armatos inciderit, corporis sui custodias arbitrabitur esse: ac si quod facinus contra committitur (quod rarissimum est) absque vlla spe veniae severe plectitur. Itaque ubi impunitatis spes nulla est, ibi sceleris audacia ingenerari non solet. Victus vero & vestitus parsimonia & frugalitas non potius legibus quam moribus tanta est, ut vectigat neque privatim neque publice universis civibus majus ullum esse videatur. Civitas Episcoporum dominatum diutius pertulit: sed Helvetici foederis societas anno 1500 facta paulatim pleniorem libertatem & majorem quam antea fuisset, pace totamque urbis administrationem lautiorem effecit. Equidē oeconomiam in una privata familia tantam nunquam fuisse non arbitror, quanta est in publica vectigalium, aedium, viarum, fontium, omnium belli pacisque instrumentorum totaque universae civitatis administratione, unde opes & privatim civibus singulis & publice toti civitati honestis firmisque rationibus stabilitae & fundatae sunt. Fartores cupedinarios phrygiones & consimilium delitiarum lenones Basilea nullos habet. Enimvero (quod honestissimae id est rusticae tribus Romae quondam fibigloriosum duxerunt) senatores saepe magna animi laetitia tanquam Cincinnatos & Curios é rustico opere in urbem redeuntes aspexi, & tamen quod minime imperiti opinentur,robur animi corporisque ista morum simplicitate & innocentia alitur & corroboratur.Militares itaque non tantum juventutis sed cujusque ætatis atque ordinis exercitationes certis diebus ordinariæ & quidem publico munere atque honore balistis & sclopetis celebrátur. Neque puellis interea virginibusque exercitatio sua deest: diebus profestis inter domesticarum rerum curas in incessu gestuque alacritas quædam virilis potius quà puellaris apparet.Denique Sic tibi puella occurret,
units.tr: So that the poet himself may also do us this favour on his own account. Permit me, then, gentlemen of Basel, to lay open to you simply the wishes and prayers that I have for our walks in this grove. The University of Paris has a clerics' meadow, and likewise a Field of Mars. On behalf of the wretched plight of students I obtained, together with my colleagues, an embassy to King Henry, and what I achieved is set out in the speech of that embassy. So I by no means envy this most honourable city its Elysian fields, but I earnestly wish for the University of Paris similar ones. Yet I linger too long over the recollection of my delights: let Basel be a most elegant and fertile city. Although the Council of Basel was held here from 1473 to 1490, the manners of the city are nonetheless more refined and more beautiful. For all these things, both from nature and from human art and industry, are most pleasant and agreeable to strangers; how much more pleasant and agreeable we may judge them to be when they see a city so governed by the evangelical religion and piety that those who live justly and uprightly in it have nothing to fear except God and the holy laws. A chest of gold and silver may lie open even with the doors unguarded: no theft is feared. A maiden, however beautiful and exceptional in form, fears no violence from a ravisher. An unarmed man who, on a dark night, meets armed men will think himself guarded by his own person. And if any crime is committed (which is very rare), it is punished severely, with no hope of pardon. Thus where there is no hope of escaping punishment, the boldness of wickedness is not commonly bred. Moreover, the frugality and simplicity of food and clothing are so great, owing to custom rather than law, that no one, either privately or publicly, seems to have more than any of the citizens. The city bore the rule of its bishops for a long time, but the alliance of the Helvetic confederation, made in 1500, gradually brought a fuller freedom, greater than before, and, with peace, a more generous administration of the whole city. Indeed, I do not think there has ever been such household management in a single private family as there is in the public management of revenues, buildings, roads, springs, all the instruments of war and peace, and the whole administration of the entire city. From this, wealth is established and founded, both for individual citizens privately and for the whole city publicly, on honest and firm principles. Basel has no sellers of pastries, no makers of embroidered trifles, no pimps of such delights. Truly, what the most honourable rustic tribes once at Rome counted as their glory, I have often seen senators, with great joy of mind, returning to the city from rural labour like Cincinnatus and Curius; and yet, as those who are not at all inexperienced suppose, the strength of body and mind is nourished and strengthened by this simplicity and innocence of manners. Accordingly, military exercises with crossbows and muskets are practised on fixed days, not only by the young but by every age and rank, as a regular public duty and honour. Meanwhile the girls and maidens do not lack their own exercise: on working days, amid the cares of household affairs, a certain manly briskness, rather than a girlish one, appears in their walk and bearing. Finally, such a maiden will meet you,

units.la: Virginis os habitumque gerens, at virginis arma Spartanæ vel qualis equos chreissa fatigat Harpalice volucremque fuga prævertitur Hebrum.
units.tr: bearing a maiden's face and bearing, but a maiden's arms, Spartan, or as the Thracian Harpalyce tires her horses, and outstrips the swift Hebrus in flight.

units.la: Ifq; in nubili virgine vigor pro civitatis moribus permagno tanquam dotis loco est ad nuptias conciliadum. Festis diebus choreę & saltationes sunt in prepatulo pudicis carminibus nullo mare permisto.Sic mollitie, otio, lasciviaque rejectis robustiorum liberorum matres efficiantur. Sed tamen ista (ut sunt) ita splendida & magnifica sunto, quanto illud magistratibus primariis splendidius & magnificentius existimamus non solum in tribunali civibus suis jus expedite promptequeq reddere, sed in medio foro consulendi sui copiam omnibus facere? ea enim laus Catonis fuit:imo vero per præcipuas urbis vias certis diebus obambulare, ac velut unamquamque familiam interrogare nunqua vel vi vel injuria vel controuersia vel difficultate alia præmatur,ad quam debij. pellendam vel explicandam magistratus authoritate'sit[?] opus, quanto (inquam) splendidius istud & magnifi-centius existimamus? Hæc me judice de Basiliensium Catonum laudibus unica, singularis & eximia fuerit. Sic astream illam justitiæ apud Poëtas deam cum in terris a-geret, verisimile est hominibus jus dixisse: & tamen ad hanc tam sanctam jurisdictionem in privatis causis ju-ris periti & consulti nulli adhibentur, neque omnino le-gum doctoratum laureamque adeptus ullus hodie est in senatu. Si quis controversi juris nodus inter judicandum inciderit, quod rarum est, jurisconsultus pro tota civita-te unicus (ut antea pater Bonifacius Amerbachius & ho-die filius Basilius Amerbachius non solum jurispruden-tia sed vera virtutis fama civis primarius) consulitur. O felices Basilienses quantum istud esse & quam mirabile cogitatis in ea Respubliqua educatis, in qua an-nus aliquando etiam decennium ad fores judiciis ante conteritur quam audientia exponendique sui juris ve-nia possit impetrari? Dixit Plato miseras esse Resp. quæ judicum multitudine abundarent: Ecquid de nostra Ba-silea dicturus fuerat, si unicum in ea jurisconsultum & quidem perpaucis horis anno toto occupatum animad-vertisset? Itaque tam moderato sanctoque imperio civi-tas consequitur, ut nullæ contumeliæ verborum, nullæ per seditionem injuriæ exoriantur, aut exortæ unico verbo (Frid) publicæ pacis veluti Mercurio protinus acquiescant. Virgilianum videlicet illud esse dixeris,
units.tr: And in an unmarried girl vigour, according to the customs of the city, is esteemed as almost a dowry for winning a marriage. On festival days there are dances and choral songs in public, with modest songs and no mixing of the sexes. Thus, with softness, idleness and wantonness cast aside, the mothers of stronger children are made. But let those things, as they are, be counted as splendid and magnificent; how much more splendid and magnificent do we judge it for the chief magistrates not only to dispense justice promptly and readily to their citizens from the tribunal, but to give everyone the opportunity of consulting them in the middle of the forum? For this was the praise of Cato. Indeed, to walk about the principal streets of the city on fixed days, and, as it were, to ask each family whether it is not oppressed by violence, injury, quarrel or some other difficulty, which needs the authority of the magistrate to drive off or resolve, how much more splendid and magnificent (I say) do we judge that to be? In my judgement this would be the unique, singular and outstanding praise of the Basel Catos. Just as Astraea, the goddess of justice whom the poets speak of, when she lived on earth, probably gave judgement to men, so too, in this so holy jurisdiction, no jurists or consultants are called in for private cases, nor does anyone today in the Senate hold the doctorate or laurel of law at all. If any knot of contested law arises in judging, which is rare, one jurist is consulted for the whole city, the only one (as formerly the father Bonifacius Amerbach, and today his son Basilius Amerbach, a leading citizen not only for his jurisprudence but for the true fame of his virtue). O fortunate Baselers, how much and how wonderful do you think that is, you who are brought up in a commonwealth in which, sometimes for a year or even ten, people wear themselves out at the doors of the courts before they can obtain a hearing and permission to set out their right! Plato said that those commonwealths are wretched which abound in a multitude of judges. What would he have said of our Basel, had he noticed that it had a single jurist, and one who is occupied all year only for a few hours? And so the city attains such a moderate and holy rule that no insults of words arise, no injuries through sedition, or, if they have arisen, they straightway give way at a single word, "Peace!", like the public peace of Mercury. You would say, of course, that this is that line of Virgil:
He yielded to God, and with his voice he stilled the battles.

units.la: Atque tam pacatam tamque pręsentem iuris æquitatem & facilitatem par comitas in peregrinos & humanitas eadem consequitur, venerint ex omnibus Europæ regionibus Britanni, Hispani, Itali, Germani: Basilea erga omnes est pereque humana & Hospitalis & táquam hominum patria quædam communis ut non jam à Gallico trajectu, sed ab omnium gentium portu iustissime Basilea nominata sit. Hęc tanta civitatis civiumque bona non dubito quin mira plerisque videantur. Sed heus qui ista admiraris, consiste & erectis sursum oculis solem syderaque reliqua circumspice, non eundem cursum Basiliensibus ac reliquis gentibus efficere videbuntur. Sol hora ante integra Basiliensibus exoritur, quam in eodem horizonte vel reliquis populis. Itaque quo tempore horologia vel umbris vel sonis Basileæ sextam significant, tum quinta vel in vicinis urbibus significatur. Huius táti miraculi caussæ [?]à quibusdam philosophis exquisitę variæ sunt. Quidam cum ad horam inter proditores dictam urbis prodenda esset, horam ipsam mirabiliter aiunt antevertisse: alii joculatoriam caussam é Basiliensi concilio comminiscuntur, ut Abbates, Episcopi, Cardinales maturius accuberent, horologia sic accelerasse at potius optato non humanum hoc esse commentum, sed cæli Basileam suam benigniore quodam aspectu intuentis pręcipuam gratiam esse. Basilea ita me Deus amet si civium frequentiam talis & soli & cæli commoditatibus exercendis idoneam aliquando nancisscatur non solum Germaniæ Argentinam, Noribergam, Augustam, sed Galliæ Rhotomagum, Lugdunum, Lutetiam, sed Italiæ Mediolanum, Venetias, Romam denique ipsam superabit, tumque nominis sui veritatem maximo atque amplissimo Germaniæ, Galliæ, Italiæ, non trajectu solum sed appulsu commeatuque complebit. Considerate (viri Ba-silienses) quibus incrementis urbes illæ capita mundi fa-cta sint, eadem suscipite: solum cælumque sed supra cætera tranquilla libertas Basileam civitatum maximam, celeberrimamque civitatem facient. Sed simile de tam copiosa laudis materia quædā amputare, pars enim propositi permagna superest. Etenim inter egregias Basilie-sium[?] laudes academia non mediocrem sibi locum vendicabit. Ditio urbis profua virtute augustis finibus con-tinetur, & pleraque superiora illa innocentiæ, modera-tionis, fortitudinis, justitiæ encomia, cum tota fœderato-rum ac sociorum Helvetiorum civitate communia vi-deri possunt. At academiæ variis linguis atque artibus per Europam universam Augustum quoddam inclytæ Basileæ nomen dilatatur & propagatur. Neque tam va-riæ tam multarum disciplinarum professiones, tot excel-lentium ingeniorum dotes ac virtutes, cum pagis reliquis communicari possunt. Ecquis igitur princeps authorque tanti tamque cœlestis boni, quis rauracæ gentis bonus genius Basiliensis academiæ parens primusque conditor fuit? Æneas Sylvius (inquam) qui Romanum pontificatum adeptus Pius secundus dictus est, hic nostræ Romæ Romulus fuit. Hic enim Basiliensium erga se humanitatem recordatus, quod ipsum cum Basiliensis cōcilii scriba esset, peste laborantem, summo studio officioque fovis-sent ac recreassent, academia omnibus laudandarum professionum privilegiis ornata tam bene meritam de sc[?] civitatem decorauit, non frustra auguratus Basileam ut aitris[?] clementia frugumque omnium ubertate & copia, ut singulari quadam vitę integritate, sic ingeniorum nobilitate memorabilem futuram. Ziboliorum Basiliensium familia deinde gymnasia (quæ hodieque sunt) ædi-ficavit. Ager tamen ille ingenii ac doctrinæ licet natura fœcundus ac fertilis, legitima tamen cultura ante evangelii adventum fere caruit, neque quicquam memorandum tulit: at simulatque vera pietas ac religio in urbem ingressa est, aut certe de ipsius ingressu agi cœptum est, mirabile sit enumerare & quot & quam excelletes omni genere eruditionis homines Basiliensis academia extulerit. Vultis igitur per genera disciplinarum delectus iste tot laudum virtutumque etsi vobis notissimus, attamen commemoratione & recordatione non ingratus recen-featur[?]. Sic opinor. A Grammaticis igitur ordiamur. Henricus Loritus Glareanus prima eruditionis fundamenta in puerili gymnasio ita posuit, ut deinde tamen ad summa cujusvis doctrinæ fastigia perduxerit: neque enim tantum Donati Grammatica partibus omnibus ab eo est explicata, sed Poëtæ & historici fere generum omnium sunt illustrati: Terentius, Horatius, Ouidius, Salustius, Cæsar, Livius, Suetonius, Halicarnasseus, Valerius:é Mathematicis etiam Arithmetica, Musica, Cosmographia ejusdem ingenii monumeta[?] sunt, Hermannus Buschius PasiphiPafiphilus Glareano nihil admodum concesserit: Donatus illustratus comparatis veteribus reliquis Grammaticis,item Poëtę plerique Plautus,Perfius,Silius,Martialis:sacræ literę variis operibus explicatæ eruditam Buschii industriam demonftrarunt. Ioannes Atrocianus in hac professione scripsit elegiam de bello rustico & epigrammata quædam:item scholia in Macrum.XyftusBetuleius eruditis in Ciceronem plurimis, nonnullis etiam in fybillina oracula commentariis, symphonia novi testamenti clarissimus, Bafilienfis etiam juventutis informator fuit. His Thomas Platerus successit uberrimi seminarii proventu cum innumerabiles annorum plurimorum tempore grammaticos genuit : tum filium felicem Platerum sic informavit,ut filii exemplo, singularis patris doctrina possit intelligi: perspexi enim & collaudavi singulare felicis ingenium atque ad omnes artes mirifico naturæ impetu incitatum : tornandi artifex,sed animi caussa,singularis est,est & fundendi artifex singularis,sed medicinæ quam facit,gratia : anatomica plerasque studiosius digessit, herbarum ac stirpium infinitam copiam ac fylvam quotidie novam exquirit,ut ad Nicolaum Deneu Parifienfem chirurgum & ῥιζοτόμον[?] regium, laude ista longe mortalium omnium ( de quibus audierim)facile principem proxime videatur accedere. Quare felice tali filio felicem & patrem meritissimo jure existimo. Ioan. Oporinus in hujus palmæ studio meditationes nobiles ostendit editis scholiis in Solinum, Ciceronem, Demosthene: multo vero nobiliores ostensurus nisi Typographiæ uberiorem quandam divitioremque palmam sibi proposuisset. Iacobus Hertelius comico-rum græcorum sententias collegit. Atque hæc gramma-tica primæ institutionis lumina quibus (quæso vos) Eu-ropæ scholis non illuxerunt? Sed nos á[?] puerilis umbra-culi ludo in sui theatri scenam Rhenis advocat: hic pu-blicas majorum & splendidiorum studiorum professio-nes ostentat: hic enim omnes humanitatis fontes latina lingua primum aperti sunt, in eaque laude princeps eni-tuit Simon Grynæus, Rhetoricæ, Dialecticæ, Geometriç professione, conversione variorum operum Plutarchi & Aristotelis, sed incredibiles omnium literarum vigiliæ præpositis in præstantissimos quosque authores commendationibus apparuerunt, ut planum inde sit singu-lari quodam fato ad liberalium artium studia excitan-dum & augendum tale ingenium natum fuisse. Alter est á Grynæo Cælius Secundus Curio in eandem humani-tatis cathedram cooptatus, cujus viri laudes omnes si-[?] numerare instituam,
units.tr: And from this so settled and so readily available justice and ease, an equal courtesy and humanity towards foreigners follows, so that Britons, Spaniards, Italians and Germans come from every region of Europe. Basel is equally humane and hospitable to all, and like a common homeland of humankind, so that it has been named Basel most justly, not only from the Gallic crossing but as the harbour of all nations. I do not doubt that these great goods of the city and its citizens will seem remarkable to many. But you there, who wonder at these things, stop, lift your eyes, and look around at the sun and the other stars: they will seem not to keep the same course for the people of Basel as for other nations. The sun rises for the Baslers a full hour earlier than it does on the same horizon for other peoples. So when the clocks in Basel strike six, by their shadows or their chimes, it is five in the neighbouring cities. Various philosophers have sought out the causes of this great marvel. Some say that when the hour was set for the city to be betrayed by traitors, the hour itself miraculously came early. Others invent a jesting cause from the Council of Basel: that the abbots, bishops and cardinals might recline at table sooner, and so the clocks were hurried along. But this is no human invention, they say; rather it is the special favour of a heaven that looks upon Basel with a kinder countenance. So may God love me, Basel, if ever it attains a crowd of citizens suited to making the most of the advantages of sun and sky, it will surpass not only Strasbourg, Nuremberg and Augsburg in Germany, but Rouen, Lyon and Paris in France, and in Italy Milan, Venice and finally Rome itself. Then it will fulfil the truth of its name, filling Germany, France and Italy not only by crossing but by arrival and traffic. Consider, men of Basel, by what increases those cities became the capitals of the world, and take up the same: the soil and sky, but above all a peaceful liberty, will make Basel the greatest and most famous of cities. But I must cut short such a copious store of praise, for by far the greater part of my purpose still remains. For among the outstanding praises of Basel, the academy will claim no small place. The territory of the city is confined within noble borders by its valour, and most of those earlier encomia of innocence, moderation, courage and justice can be seen as shared with the whole state of the allied and confederate Swiss. But through the academy, in various languages and arts, the august name of famous Basel is spread and propagated throughout all Europe. Nor can such varied and numerous professions of many disciplines, and such gifts and virtues of so many excellent minds, be shared with the other villages. Who then was the prince and author of so great and so heavenly a good? Who was the good genius of the Rauraci, the parent and first founder of the Basel academy? Aeneas Sylvius (I say), who attained the Roman papacy and was called Pius II, was the Romulus of our Rome here. For he, remembering the kindness of the Baslers towards himself, when he was secretary of the Council of Basel and was suffering from the plague, had been cherished and restored with the greatest zeal and service; so he adorned the city, so well deserving of him, by founding an academy furnished with privileges for every praiseworthy profession. He had rightly foreseen that Basel would be remarkable, as much for the mildness of its air and its abundance of all crops as for a singular integrity of life and the nobility of its talents. The Zibol family of Basel afterwards built the gymnasia (which still stand today). Yet that field of talent and learning, though naturally fertile and rich, lacked proper cultivation before the coming of the gospel and brought forth nothing worth recording. But as soon as true piety and religion entered the city, or at least when its entry began to be discussed, it is wonderful to list how many and how excellent men of every kind of learning the Basel academy has produced. Would you therefore like, through the kinds of disciplines, this selection of so many praises and virtues, though very well known to you, to be reviewed in recollection and remembrance, not unwelcome? So I think. Let us begin, then, with the grammarians. Henricus Loritus Glareanus laid the first foundations of learning in the boys' school, and yet afterwards led them up to the highest summits of every branch of learning. For he explained not only Donatus's grammar in all its parts, but illustrated almost all kinds of poets and historians: Terence, Horace, Ovid, Sallust, Caesar, Livy, Suetonius, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Valerius. Among the mathematicians, arithmetic, music and cosmography are monuments of the same mind. Hermann Buschius (Pasiphilus) yielded nothing at all to Glareanus: Donatus was illustrated, the other ancient grammarians compared, and most poets, Plautus, Persius, Silius, Martial, and the sacred writings explicated in various works, demonstrated the learned industry of Buschius. Johannes Atrocianus in this profession wrote an elegy on the Peasants' War, some epigrams, and likewise scholia on Macer. Xystus Betuleius, very learned in Cicero with many commentaries, and some also on the Sibylline oracles, a most distinguished harmonist of the New Testament, was also a teacher of the Basel youth. After these, Thomas Platerus succeeded, a rich source of a fruitful seminary, since in countless years he produced grammarians in great numbers; and he so trained his son, the gifted Platerus, that in the son's example the singular learning of the father can be understood. For I have observed and praised the singular talent of Felix, and his mind, driven by a marvellous natural impetus towards all the arts: he is a singular craftsman in turning, but for his own pleasure; he is also a singular craftsman in casting, but his cast is for medicine. He has studied anatomy more diligently than most, and every day he seeks out an infinite store and forest of herbs and plants, new each day, so that by this praise he seems to come very near, indeed almost to be first, among all mortals (of whom I have heard), to Nicolas Deneu, the Parisian surgeon and royal root-cutter. Therefore, I rightly think the father is fortunate in having such a fortunate son. Johannes Oporinus, in the pursuit of this palm, showed noble meditations in his published scholia on Solinus, Cicero and Demosthenes; but he would have shown far nobler ones, had he not proposed to himself a richer and more abundant palm in printing. Jacobus Hertelius collected the sayings of the Greek comic poets. And these are the lights of the grammar of first instruction, by which (I ask you) have they not shone upon the schools of Europe? But the boyish little shadow-play summons us to the stage of its theatre on the Rhine: here it displays the public professions of the greater and more splendid studies. For here all the sources of humanity were first opened in the Latin language, and in this praise Simon Grynaeus shone as leader, in the profession of rhetoric, dialectic and geometry, in translating various works of Plutarch and Aristotle. But his incredible vigils over all literature appeared in the commendations prefixed to the most excellent authors, so that it is plain that such a talent was born by a singular fate to stir up and advance the study of the liberal arts. The second after Grynaeus is Caelius Secundus Curio, co-opted into the same chair of humanity; if I were to undertake to enumerate all the praises of this man,
I would try to count the waves of the Icarian sea.

units.la: Etenim primas artes loquendi, dicendi, differendi, variis præceptis instructas requiris? Cælius instruxit: Ci-ceronis topica partitiones, Brutum, item varias orationes diligenter & erudite exposuit, totamque linguæ latinæ copiam & ubertatem usu quodam pleniore in Ciceronis thesauro foroque Romano patefecit. Historiæ multiplicis varia lectione delectaris? Cælius supplemen-tum fabellico addidit, Bellum melitense conscripsit, Guiciardinum latine convertit, castigationes excellen-tium scriptorum & illustrationes, præfationes, epistolas, orationes varias atq; utiles, aliasque generis hujus commentationes é Græco & Italico publicavit. Neque vero linguæ difertioris ea tantum à Cælio beneficia sunt, sed vitæ sanctioris ornamenta longe sunt excellentiora: de corruptæ ecclesiæ statu, de vera ecclesiæ Christi authori-tate, de providentia Dei divinique regni amplitudine deque tota christianæ religionis institutione. Quapro-pter quandiu homines erunt qui latine loquentur aut intelligent, tandiu humanitatis grata erga Grynæum & Cælium memoria extabit. Quid græcæ orationis profes-sio, quibus professoribus celebranda ac prædicanda est? De Grynæo jam dixi. Sebastianus Castellio & Theodo-rus Zuingerus par alterum nobile fecit [?]. Castellio con-versionibus præcipue delectatus est: convertit latine Xe-nophontis & é Iosepho Mosis Rempub. quædam etiam Cyrilli, sacra item biblia, dialogos autem sacros oratio-ne prosa, versu etiam sibyllina oracula, aliquotque Da-vidis odas conscripsit: atque utinam tanti ingenii taque [?] bonis artibus ac literis eruditi vis illa in hoc unico græ-cæ professionis argumento versari maluisset, nihil mea quidem sententia in isto genere laudis Basilea compa-randum habuisset Zuingerus Castellioni successit no-stræ quondam scholæ alumnus, & ideo verecundius vo-ce nostra memorandus, ne magister é discipuli studiis laudem repetere videatur: sed tamen accurata græcæ li-teraturæ professio studiosis fructuosa, academiæ univer-sæ honorifica. sæ honorifica, civibus perjucunda: sed multo magis humanæ vitę theatrum laboris infiniti ex infinitis authoribus conflatum: sed quoniam medicinæ se præcipue dedidit, Galenus præcipuis partibus, Hippocrates totus Zuingeri industriam doctrinamque etiam tacente me, amplissime demonstrabunt. Ad Hebraicam itaque sacrę linguę professionem venio in qua Sebastianus Munsterus tam multa tanque præclara monimenta edidit ut vel ad nomina librorum recensenda libro pene sit opus: sed ingenii fœcunditas etiam in historiarum & mathematum fines latissime redundavit, hinc historię conversę, hinc horologia, organum uranicum, canones luminarium, geographicę in Melam & Solinum commentationes, sed geographia etiam separato prægrandi opere demonstrant hoc Basiliesis Varronis ingenium κέρας ἀμαλθείας insigne quoddam fuisse. Sebastianus Lepusculus Munstero successit facilitate in docendo familiari, ut si me cursus studiorum ad has literas advocarit, talem imprimis doctorem mihi contingere cupiā. Quamobrem (viri Basilienses) gratis (opinor) animis recordamini vel imprimis academię vestrę incunabulis quanta doctrinę nobilitas, quantaque præstantia reperiatur: sed incunabula ista reliquarum etiam ætatum maturitatem & gravitatem complexa sunt. Et tamen é professionibus reliquis multo amplior gloria.
units.tr: For do you require the first arts of speaking, of oratory and of disputation, furnished with various precepts? Caelius furnished them: he carefully and learnedly expounded Cicero's Topics and Partitions, the Brutus, and various orations, and through a fuller practice in Cicero's treasury and the Roman forum he laid open the whole copia and richness of the Latin tongue. Are you delighted by the varied reading of many kinds of history? Caelius added a supplement to Fabellicus, wrote the Melitene War, translated Guicciardini into Latin, and published corrections and illustrations of excellent writers, prefaces, letters, various and useful orations, and other commentaries of this kind from Greek and Italian. Nor are these benefits from Caelius confined to the more eloquent language; the ornaments of a holier life are far more excellent: on the state of the corrupted Church, on the true authority of the Church of Christ, on the providence of God and the amplitude of the divine kingdom, and on the whole institution of the Christian religion. Therefore, as long as there are men who speak or understand Latin, so long will the grateful memory of humanity towards Grynaeus and Caelius endure. What of the profession of Greek oratory, and by what teachers is it to be celebrated and proclaimed? Of Grynaeus I have already spoken. Sebastianus Castellio and Theodorus Zwinger made a second noble pair. Castellio took especial delight in translations: he translated into Latin some of Xenophon, and of Josephus the Mosaic Republic, also some of Cyril, likewise the sacred Bible; and he wrote sacred dialogues in prose, and in verse the Sibylline oracles and some odes of David. And would that that force of so great a talent and so learned in good arts and letters had preferred to be employed in this single subject of Greek learning: in my opinion Basel would have had nothing to match in that kind of praise. Zwinger succeeded Castellio, a former pupil of our school, and therefore he is to be mentioned with more modesty by our voice, lest the teacher seem to seek praise from the studies of his pupil. Yet the careful profession of Greek literature is fruitful to students, honourable to the whole academy, and most pleasing to citizens; but far more it is a theatre of infinite labour for human life, compiled from infinite authors. But since he devoted himself above all to medicine, Galen in his principal parts and Hippocrates entire will amply demonstrate Zwinger's industry and learning, even if I say nothing. So I come to the profession of the Hebrew language, in which Sebastian Münster published so many and such famous monuments that merely to list the names of the books would almost be the work of a volume. But the fruitfulness of his talent overflowed most widely into the fields of history and mathematics: hence translated histories, hence clocks, the uranic instrument, tables of the luminaries, geographical commentaries on Mela and Solinus; and geography too, in a separate very large work, shows that the talent of this Basel Varro was a notable horn of Amalthea. Sebastian Lepusculus succeeded Münster, with a facility in teaching so familiar that, if the course of my studies should call me to these letters, I would above all desire to have such a teacher. Therefore, men of Basel, you will recall with gladness, I think, especially in the cradle of your academy, how great the nobility of learning and how great the distinction that is found there; but those cradles have also embraced the maturity and weight of the later ages. And yet the glory of the other professions is far greater.

units.la: Rhetoricam docere cœperat Cælius Augustinus Curio Cæli secundi F. adolescens naturę indole magis omnibus admirabili quam cuique credibilis attamen exposita ante oculos monimenta, hieroglyphicorum libri duo, farracenicæ historiæ libri tres, de regno marochensi unus, de vita obituque quatuor fororum unus, locupletissimam fidem faciunt ingenii supra ętatem supraque hominum expectationem eruditi: anno siquidem octavo & vicesimo extinctus est, paternæ gloriæ patrimonium longe lateque propagaturus, si naturalem vitæ cursum hęc dona tulissent, verum
units.tr: Caelius Augustinus Curio, son of Caelius Secundus Curio, a young man of a natural talent more wonderful than anyone could credit, had begun to teach rhetoric. The monuments he left behind, two books of hieroglyphics, three books of Saracen history, one book on the kingdom of Morocco, and one on the life and death of four sisters, give the fullest proof of a learning beyond his years and beyond all human expectation. For in his twenty-eighth year he was snatched away, just when he was about to spread his father's glory far and wide, had these gifts been allowed a natural span of life. But

units.la: Ostendunt terris hunc tantum fata nec ultra Esse sinunt.
units.tr: The Fates show him to the earth alone, and do not allow him to remain any longer.

units.la: Ioannes Thomas Freigius Rhetoricę secundus à Cęlio filio professor est, minime tamen professionis humanitate contentus, altiorem iurisprudentię facultatem consequutus, pro ętate spem facit ampliorum vigiliarum. Quid Dialecticę professio quantos viros habet? Philippus Bechius studiose & laboriose teneram iuventutem erudiuit, & Pachymerium é græco convertit. Ioan. Fieglinus differendi facultatem in schola sic instituit, ut in sacris concionibus eloquentiam populo admirabilem faciat. Tu vero (mi Ioan. Hospiniane) non solum literis latinis & græcis, sed assiduis in Aristotelis organo vigiliis & editis & meditatis, sed professionis fide, sed officii quadam religione egregiam laudem consequutus es: sed tu tuique professionis hujus collegę cęteri partibus infinitis ampliorem laudem consequemini, si dialecticum ut artificium, sic artificii usum in Virgilio & Homero, in Cicerone & Demosthene iuventuti proponatis, & quotidianę imitationis exeplo & opere informetis: partiamini tempora professionis logicę, minimam temporis partem logicę præceptis, maximam usui, meo cōsilio, tribuetis, sin vobis Aristotelis judicium atque exeplum luculentius est, professionis partem philosophiæ & præceptis,partem eloquentiæ & exemplis assignabitis,ut tamen memineritis usum artis, non artem usus finem esse: nec interea leges academiæ vereamini: academia enim pro ista culpa ( qua pro logica mortua in libris, vivam in ipso opere logico , proque plumbea auream feceritis) præmium coronamque decernet: vobisque authoribus Rhodolphos Agricola Basileam adductos liberali gratoque animo accipiet. Verumenimvero tempora me deficient, si reliquarum professionum laudes persequi instituam. Mathematum gloriam in plerisque attigimus. Volfangus Vissemburgius descriptionem terræ sanctæ, geographię ptolemaicæ instaurationem patriæ illustrationem, animi a grauioribus sancti ministerii curis recreandi causa sibi propositi. Christianus Vurstisius editis in ipso professionis initio problematis astrologicis pignus ingenii præclara quædam meditantis esse voluit. Enimvero ne quam liberalis disciplinæ partem á Basiliensi academia abesse suspiceris, musica hic etiam ordinaria professio instituta est, qua graviores cæterorum studiorum musæ ad Pythagoreum morem recreentur: Themistocles in convivio cum Lyram recusasset, habitus est indoctior, Themistocles nempe literas Basileæ nequaquam didicerat. Quid tum vero physica reliqua cujusmodi sunt? Certe studio virtutis nihilo sunt inferiora. Etenim Hieronymus Gemuseus si requiras quantum physicis rebus lucis & splendoris attulerit, de-clarabunt praefationes in Aristotelis, & Theophrasti opera: sed ingenii pleniorem ubertatem praefatio in Ptolo-meum, Strabonis conversio plenius ostentabunt. Henricus Pantaleon adolescens comediam scripsit Zacheum: post etiam prodita chronographia & prosopographia in eadem professione nihil humilius affectavit. Una reli-qua professio est e philosophicis, ethica quam Hulderi-cus Mutius Hugovaldus ea diligentia profitetur, ut si li-bri omnes ethici interiissent, memoriter & ad verbum possit restituere. Hujus nomen apud exteros etiam praeclarum est, quod ipse de suis studiis libro & epistola ad eos, qui Christum ex animo quaesierunt, itemque de Ger-manorum prima origine, moribus, institutis & legibus, aliisque memorabilibus pace & bello gestis celebravit. Atque haec infima publicarum professionum veluti clas-sis est, Quid medicorum, jureconsultorum, Theologo-rum professiones quales adhuc fuerunt?
units.tr: John Thomas Freigius, son of Caelius, is the second professor of rhetoric. He is not content with the humanities alone, but has also taken up the higher faculty of law, and at his age he holds out hope of greater labours to come. What great men the chair of dialectic has had! Philip Bech studied and laboured diligently in teaching the tender youth, and he translated Pachymeres from the Greek. John Fiegelin set up the teaching of disputation in the school so that he makes his eloquence admired by the people in the sacred sermons. But you, my dear John Hospinian, have won an outstanding praise, not only by your Latin and Greek learning, but by your constant nightly labours, both published and meditated, on the Organon of Aristotle, and by your fidelity to your profession and a certain conscientiousness in your duty. Yet you and your fellow professors of this chair will win far greater praise on countless counts, if you set dialectic before the young as an art, and the use of that art in Virgil and Homer, in Cicero and Demosthenes, and form them by daily imitation and practice. Divide the time of the logic lectures: in my judgement, give the smallest part to the precepts of logic and the largest to its use. But if Aristotle's judgement and example seem to you clearer, then assign part of the course to the precepts of philosophy and part to eloquence and its examples, though remember that the use of an art, not the art itself, is the end. Nor should you fear the statutes of the university in the meantime: for the university, for that fault (by which you will have made logic dead in books rather than alive in the logical work itself, and bronze instead of gold), will decree a reward and a crown; and at your recommendation it will receive with a generous and grateful mind Rudolf Agricola, brought to Basel. Indeed time would fail me if I were to pursue the praises of the other professions. We have touched on the glory of the mathematicians in most cases. Wolfgang Wissenburg has written a description of the Holy Land and a restoration of Ptolemy's geography, and an illustration of his fatherland, which he undertook to refresh his mind from the heavier cares of the holy ministry. Christian Wurstisen, by publishing astrological problems at the very beginning of his professorship, wished to show a pledge of a mind meditating on distinguished things. Indeed, lest you suspect that any part of the liberal arts is absent from the Basel academy, an ordinary professorship of music has also been established here, by which the more serious Muses of the other studies are refreshed in the manner of Pythagoras: when Themistocles at a banquet refused the lyre, he was thought unlearned, for Themistocles had certainly not learned letters at Basel. What then of the rest of the natural sciences? Surely they are in no way inferior in the pursuit of virtue. For if you ask how much light and splendour Jerome Gemusaeus has brought to natural things, the prefaces to his works on Aristotle and Theophrastus will declare it; but the prefaces to Ptolemy and his translation of Strabo will show more fully the fuller richness of his talent. Henry Pantaleon as a young man wrote the comedy Zacheus; afterwards, having published a chronography and a prosopography, he aimed at nothing lowly in the same profession. There remains one profession among the philosophical ones: ethics, which Huldrych Mutius Hugwald teaches with such diligence that, if all the books of ethics had perished, he could restore them from memory word for word. His name is famous even among foreigners, for he himself celebrated, in a book and in a letter to those who have sought Christ with their whole heart, and likewise in a work on the earliest origin, customs, institutions and laws of the Germans, and other memorable deeds of war and peace, his own studies. And these lowest of the public professions are, as it were, the rear of the fleet. What of the professions of physicians, jurists and theologians, as they have been until now?
The unique glory of the noble physicians: Copus

units.la: Ut de praestantissimo medico praestantissimus ille vir cecinit. Hippocratem, Galenum, Aeginetam testes in dustriæ suę reliquit[?]. Osvaldus Berus[?] arcana etiam theologiæ mysteria tractavit: Albanum Torinum Aeginetæ, Philaretí, Theophili, Polybii, Epiphanii, Agapeti, Damasceni, Chrysolorę Apicii, Tralliani, Philothei conversæ vel illustratæ vigiliæ perpetuo commendabunt. Ioan. Huberus, Isaacus Collarius academiæ rector ma-gnificus professionem ordinariam summa doctrina di-ligentiaque pari sustinent ac tuentur. At me obliviosum nec satis admirabilium ingeniorum memorem. Theo-phrastum Paracelsum Bafiliensis academia medicinæ lingua germanica professorem habuit, qui in intima naturæ viscera sic penitus introierit, metallorum stir-piumque vi es. & facultates tam incredibili ingenii a-cumine exploraverit ac perviderit ad morbos omnes vel desperatos & opinione hominum insanabiles percu-randum, ut cum Theophrasto nata primum medicina perfectaque videatur. Tanta Asclepiadi fama Romæ in populo militiæ studiis dedito contigit, vt totam vete-rem medicinam abrogaret, novamque sectam conde-ret, qua sæpe vino, alias abstinentia cibi, vinique, frica-tione corporis, ambulatione, gestatione morbi omnes curarentur. Itaque cum ea fama excitos Mithridatis re-gis legatos & pollicitationes sprevisset, hominemque é [?] funere relatum servasset, universum prope hominum genus in sese convertit. Theophrastus nempe germani-cus hic Asclepiades fuit, quë [?] Adamus Abodestinus Ba-sileæ suscitat, sicuti tota Germania plerique excellentes medici. jurisprudentia medicinam sequitur, illustrium jurisprudentium fama ac dignitate percelebris. Etenim Claudius Cantiuncula Dialecticam juris prudenti ne-cessariam esse jurisprudentiæ [?] exemplis docuit, Iustiniani libros quosdam illustrauit, judicis officium descripsit, jurisprudentiam cum evangelio conjunxit. Huldricus Iselinus, Martinus Huberus Ioan.fi. Gasparus Hervagius in eadem cathedra floruerunt. Marcus Hoperus sacra-rum item literarum studio captus, Eusebii & aliorum operum sacrorum conversionibus notior est. Joannem Huldricum Zafium magni illius Zafii filium jurisprudentia Basilien-sis professorem suum fuisse permagnæ laudis loco ducit, imperatorisque Cancellarium factum sibi gratulatur. Joan. Sichardus Justiniani codicem illustravit, edidit & præfationibus commendavit authores plurimos, quos Imperatoris mandato & authoritate ex diversis bibliothecis eruerat. Nicolaus Brieferus jus civile magna cum laude docuit, sed historia imprimis excelluit. Basilius Amerbachius, Adamus Petreius, Samuel Grynæus in eam ipsam cathedram ingressi, majorum suorum stemmatis consentanea pollicentur: sed Amerbachii urbanum illud patrocinium jam dictum est, & humanitas mihi præcipuo nomine est complectenda, qui bibliothecam omni excellentium librorum genere instructam & ornatam quoties libuit, toties apertam nobis expositamque esse voluit. Et tamen cum bibliothecam tot libris ornatam suspexeris, bibliothecæ dominum, si se tibi penitus aperiat (modestia enim permagnas animi laudes veluti tectas habet) librorum lectione scientiaque ornatiorem invenies. Samuel patris effigiem præclare inchoavit, & valde confido patrimonium laudis etiam amplificaturum. Te vero Bernarde Brande senator clarissime cur in isto laudis studio prætereamnam cum honorum tuorum cursus in iis studiis ætatem tuam exercuit, te nobilem jurisprudentiæ professorem academia Basilien-sis habuit: ac nisi rei militaris potior gloria, civitatis amplior & splendidior administratio abduxisset, nobinobilissimum jurisconsultum sine dubio nunc haberet. Testabitur hoc ipsum Azonis illa summa á te repurgata & scholiis illustrata. In historia vero quid posis[?], chronica tua ab orbe condito germanicè descripta, locuples atque insigne testimonium perpetuo perhibebunt. Itaque ut patre tuo optimo prudentissimoque viro Theodoro Brando consule Basilea gloriosa est, ita filium vel ante annos consulem tacitis non tam suffragiis quam votis designat atque instituit. Ergo jurisprudentia Basiliensis tam claros tamque illustres professores adhuc habuit. Quid theologiæ professio cujusmodi aut qualisnam fuit? Theologia nempe de professionibus ordinariis ut gradu summa est, sic divinis laudibus est amplissima. Professores ordinarii duo sunt professionis genere mihi imprimis laudato atque optato. Hic Simon Sulcerus & Huldricus Coccius nobis auditi assidue atque auscultati sunt: nec enim consolatio mihi major in his civilium tempestatum miseriis ulla fuit, quam ut assiduas utriusque prælectiones auscultarem: cum alter testamentum vetus Hebraicè, alternovum Græcè interpretaretur.Tum enim voti compos fieri mihi visus sum, pro quo proœmium Parisiensis academiæ pene capitale nobis extitisset, cum nostris Theologis optarem, ut tali profesione puriorem verbi divini Theologiam é suis fontibus ita haurirent, & ita hauriendam discipulis ostenderent. Vissemburgius ante mathematica laude ornatus est, sed Theologia ampliore ornandus sit, qui explicádæ populo Romanæ religionis gratia missam[?] germanice fecerit:deinde constanti fortique animo evangelium Basileæ inter primos annuntiaverit, perpe-tuoque postea defenderit. Ubelhardus mathematum quoque studiis, sed physicis præsertim & ad vitam ac-commodatis impense delectatur,parique constantia pa-triam religionem tuetur. Sed quid virorum, de quibus etiam meliora sperari possint, præsentes cursus spectamus potius, quam defunctorum decursa stadia recorda-mur? Etenim Paulus Constantinus phrygio in hac ipsa theologica decursione imprimis enituit, editis commen-tariis in Exodum,Leviticum,Micheam,& historico stu-dio valde nobilitatus est, edita chronologia regum om-nium seriem ab origine mundi complexa. Grynæi pa-tris professionem antea celebratam nō repeto,sed theo-logicam præcipuè celebrandam esse contendo. Ho-meliæ enim Chrysostomi in latinum sermonem con-versæ, commentaria in Paulum,liber de cœna domini, sed vitæ vere theologicæ integritas & innocentia, tam luculentis studiis comes & socia, theologum insignem præstiterunt. Andreas Carolostadius studio illustrandæ dominicæ cœnę jactationem quandam habuit:sed ipsius adversus Grynæum in senatu certamen, academiæ lon-ge gratissimum, prætereundum non arbitror: Grynæi stoica illa ac fortasse verior sententia fuit, licentiatus, magisteria, doctoratus, similesque in academiis gradus inania & sophistica esse doctrinæ nomina, quæ frequen-ter indignis pretio potius addicerentur, quam vera lau-de virtutis docto & erudito cuiquam gratis attribueren-tur, tur:itaque ajebat Grynæus,qui potest docere, doceat, & ubi virtus est, illic appareat. Carolostadius contra di-sputabat examina ingeniorum & studiorum gradus esse, quibus certo probari posset,quantum quisque in libera-libus studiis progressum profectumque fecisset, & mores academiarum suæ caussæ fautores, id est valde diser-tos & populares patronos atque oratores habebat. Itaque pervicit ut insignia virtutis, sicuti corporis orna-menta,à suis velut opificibus peterentur. Martinus Bor-rhaus philosophicis & mathemathicis, sed præcipue theologicis vigiliis & professione inter primarios theo-logos habitus est. Quid Osvaldum Myconium quanta eruditio doctrinæ, quantaque vitæ sanctitas exornavit? Helvetiam Glareani juvenis illustravit, vitam & obi-tum Huldrici Zuinglii memoriæ tradidit, Beati Marci evangelium itemque psalmum 16i docte pieque expo-suit. Oecolampadii sacra aliquot opera præfationibus commendavit, eiusque catechisinum latinum fecit: scripsit & alia permulta. Verumenimvero Ioan. Oeco-lampadius laudis hujus & primas & summas partes facil-lime obtinet, literis latinis, græcis, hebraicis sic instru-ctus & ornatus, ut in hoc tantum studio tota vita illi consumpta videretur: & tamen conversis é gæco præser-tim Chrysostomo,Nazianzeno, Nicephoro, Theophy-lacto, & plerisque aliis, tam multæ, tam variæ, tamque multiplices in Prophetarum & Apostolorum oracula e-lucubrationes & vigiliæ,commentationes tot tantarum-que cōtentionum literis & latinis & germanicis, totque conciones editę sunt, ut diligetissimi lectoris vita videa-tur opus ad scripta tam varia perlegendum. Et tamen la-bores istos tam herculeos quotam mirabilis ingenii partem esse arbitramur. Adversus religionis mostra (quæ tum in hac civitate sicut in reliquis Europæ civitatibus inveteraverant, vigilandum, consistendum, in acie, dies ac noctes non solum manu & lingua, sed sancta imprimis & incorrupta vita dimicandum fuit. Neque hic vul-gare quicquam aut cum multis commune prædico. Ete-nim in cęteris ętatis memorięque nostrę quamvis excel-lentibus theologis æstus tamen aliquis ardorque vehe-metius nescio quid interdum excitavit, quod etiam ipsis postea sedatioribus factis displiceret. Oecolampadii constatia & sua sibi similis æquabilitas immutabilis per-petuo permansit. Maxima vero omnium & gravissima concertatio de cœna Domini fuit, ut ad veritatem per-duceret, quam cofesio Basiliensis Oecolampadio mor-tuo (ne quis hypocrita perverteret) senatus mādato ger-manice edita sanxit atque approbavit. Et certe ad extre-mum usque vitæ diem cum Tigurino illo Hervetię gen-tis heroe altero adversus errorem tam gravem ita con-certavit, ut suam spartam labe religionis maculaque pu-ram mundam que relinqueret. Ergo (viri Basilienses) Deus hunc vobis Prophetā suscitavit, per quem ad evan-gelii sui cognitione vos adduceret, eius doctrinam grata piaq; memoria retinete, vestris animis insitā penitus at-que impressā conservate, studiosq; perspicite ne bono-rum omnium maximum ac præstantissimum vobis eri-piatur. piatur. Annales vestri loquuntur quanta Basiliensium constátia pro Ludovico Bavaro adversus Romani pontificis terrifica fulmina fuerit, ut ipsum dirarum præconem é mariana rupe in Rhenum pręcipitarint:& memoria recenti vivaque Iacobus Mejerus Basiliensis consul Oecolampadio clypeus & hasta fuit in asserenda evangelii libertate:Mejeros in cŏservanda ac retinenda constantes & fortes habetis, atque in perpetuum meis votis habetote.Equidem cum in dominicana ambulatione illam mortis choream prætereiens egregio pictoris artificio oculos pascerē, valde lætatus sum Oecolampadium mortalibus omnibus ad bene moriedum doctorem vestro jussu tam eleganter expressum esse: id enim credo vos in tali monimeto spectasse,ut nō solu docti,sed pueri mulierculæ, sed bajuli & remiges, sed quâlibet illiteratum vulgus pictura illa tamen admonitum reminiscere-tur hunc virum christianæ libertatis authorem vestris civibus extitisse, domesticamque illam purioris religionis lampadem Basiliensibus illuxisse. O pastorem grege tam memori tamque liberali vero fortunatum:imo vero ó gregem pastore tam excellenti tamque singulari vere beatum. Sed á diuino isto Oecolampadii animo divelli non possũ, deque eo vehemetius cogitans Ioan. Brandmulerum pene præterii, quo tamen si Oecolampadianę synceritatis germanus successor suo tempore requiratur,germaniorem equidem vix ullum Basiliensibus augurer.Itaque Brandmulere augurium nostrum doctrinæ & vitæ ut cœpisti, egregia virtute cŏfirmato. Quamobrem (viri Basilienses) recognoscitis academiam vestram tantæ dignitatis fontem quendam perennem esse: cujus etiam consuetudine & suavitate capti, præterea innumerabiles omnis doctrinæ principes (qui ordinariam profesionem nullam obierint) Basileam sempiterna laude celebrabunt. Cælius Horatius Curio Cælii filius qui annum natus decimum & quintum editis in hac urbe de amplitudine divinæ misericordiæ & aliquot declamationum libris magnam sui expectationem concitavit, sed mors eum in rerum magnarum cursu abripuit: cujus sororem Angelam præter cætera virginis ornamenta non solum Germanicè, Italicè, Gallicè, sed & latine loquutâ (quod ipsius manuscriptæ declarant epistolæ) equidem etiam ad patris eximias laudes aggrego. Ioannes Herodus qui variarum gentium historias, orationes aliquot latine, sed plura germanicè è græcis, latinis, italis convertit. Guilelmus Gratarolus medicus, qui non medica tantum sed theologica conscripsit. Io. Gastius qui historicis, poëmatis, parabolis Augustini & Hieronymi veluti floribus delibatis, sed præcipuè Oecolampadii conquisitis & digestis operibus egregium nomen reperit. Conradus Lycosthenes quam industriam in originibus patriæ in Romana antiquitate, in historicis, in infinitorum generum parabolis, apophtegmatis dictis, factis, non exprompsit? Quis vestrum oblitus est Bonifacium Amerbachium non modo Basileæ, sed universæ Germaniæ legum Romanarum sapientia velut Appollinem fuisse? & in filio Basilio Amerbachio patriam gloriam veluti hæreditareditaria successione perpetuasse? Ioannes Conon græcę linguæ singularis magister, Beatus Rhenanus, Ioannes Lafcus, Sebastianus Titio, Ioannes Reuclinus, Volfangus Capito, Conradus Gefnerus, Vrbanus Rhegius, Sigismundus Gelenius, Hieronimus Volfius, Ioânes Brentius, Conradus Pelicanus atque imprimis immortale illud Heluetiæ decus Huldricus Zuinglius, nostræ ætatis fama gloriaque academiæ quondam nostræ fama gloriaque fuerút. Desiderium veró Erafmum quis Basilien-sis academiæ tot annos potius hospitem fuisse, quá sempiternam dignitatem fore existimet? Sed inter academię Basiliêsis hospites Ioan. Calvinus præcipuè commemorandus est lumé Galliæ, lumen christianę per orbem terrarum ecclefię, lumen in hoc ipso (in quo hæc meditor commétorque) hospitio præcipue perspectum: hic enim tanti luminis faces (ut Catharina Petita lectissima matrona sanctitate singularis ingenii mirifice capta tum Calvini modo etiam Rami hospita sæpe ac jucunde mihi narravit) primum sunt incensę: hic illustres illę Christianæ institutionis cęlestesque vigilię sunt exaratę & elaboratę. Sed Calvinus gloriam suam melius ipse per se præ-dicabit, præconem alium neminem requiret. Agedum Basiliensis academiæ hospites, familiares etiam nostri in istam gratiæ gratulationisque societatem succedite, huc enim nisi Andream Penam, Petrum Castelnovum, Petrum Pitheum, Ioannem Bohinum, Cornelium Bombergam, Cassiodorum Rhemium, Franciscum Bethum, Syluestrum Teglium adjunxero, eruditæ mihi cum ipsis famifamiliaritatis & philosophicæ in quotidiana collocu-tione consuetudinis immemor parumque gratus exi-stimer. Provincia Penam & Castelnovum senatores senatus sui ornamenta suspicit. P. Pitheum jurisconsultum ipsa jurisprudentia, sed & historiæ quidam præcipuus amor, magna laudum historia commendabit. Bohinum non tantum medicina Basilien-sibus salutaris, sed popularis quædam bonitas & gratia, gratissimum efficit. Cornelius Bomberga bonis literis atque artibus nec minus bono fortique animo præditus patrium illum ac domesticum bonis literis atque artibus edendis ac publicandis honorem tueretur, nisi tempora virtutibus inimica tum vehementer obsisterent. Cassiodorum Rhennium Hispanum labor ingens atque immensus amor patriæ sacris studiis erudiendæ & ab impia ;superstitio sævitia vindicandę quamvis taceri atque ignorari velit, minime tamen tacitum atque ignotum esse patietur. Francisco Betho & Sylvestro Teglio vix Italia duos Italos candidiores & verę pietatis amantiores appos-uerit. Bethus patriam patrio sermone christianissimi sacris initiat. Teglius Machiavelli principem latine loquentem fecit, majoraque nominis sui monimeta quotidie molitur. Te vero Marce Peresi etsi Basiliesi civitate donatum tamen academiæ vel hospitam præcipuü, vel certe municipem, quibus tandem laudum argumentis appellem? Etenim opibus magnis abundare, comercia cum omnibus chri-stiani orbis gentibus perampla exercere: scire Flandrice, Germanice, Italice, Hispanice, Gallice: imo loculeter eleganter latine, liberalium artium studia coluisse, sacras imprimis literas evolvisse, de tam variis sæculo nostro tamque discrepantibus theologorum judiciis rectissima selegisse, magna quædam in te raraque ingenii atque industriæ encomia sunt, sed opibus amicos & cives tuos juvare, commercio plurimarum rerum nationibus pro-desse, linguarum communione cum tam differentibus populis doctis indoctisque scripto linguave communi-care, é religionis intelligentia non orationis ornatum, sed cultum vitæ melioris exquirere, afflicta Christianæ ecclesię membra consilio, opera, pecunia, cohortatione, periculo etiam salutis ac vitæ instruere, tueri, sustentare, consolari, propugnare, in eoque summum sibi bonum collocare, denique virtutis instrumenta ad usum virtu-tis referre, ea demum tibi solida est constansque gloria. Itaque ex infinitis urbibus urbem maxime omnium ho-spitalem merito adamasti, in qua infinitis mortalibus communem quendam beneficentiæ ac liberalitatis ho-spitem exhiberes. Verum sitaliquis[?] in laudibus academiæ nostræ modus, & tamen ex hac tot tamque præ-stantium ingeniorum parente vel hospite academia Ty-pographiam natam & educatam id est alimoniam plu-rimorum civium opulentiamque certissimam præterire non possumus.
