Hinc Amerbachii, Frobenii, Episcopii, Petrei, Curiones, Hervagii, Isingeri, Cratandri, Oporini, Bethelii, Guarini, Bryllingeri, Pernæ, cæterique nobiles Typographi Basileam non tantum opibus, sed egregia liberalis industriæ apud omnes nationes fama decorarunt. O Bafileam cum cęteris[?] civitatis commoditatibus & civium virtutibus tum academiæ singularibus tam variarum laudum nominibus inclytam.Scripsit (viri Ba-filienses) Beatus Rhenanus academiam Basilienfem minus florere, quia stipendiorum proventus pertenues & perexiguos haberet. Enimvero tenuitas & exiguitas ista suo pondere palmas generosarum mentium premere potuit, opprimere ut succumberet, non potuit. Et tamen optimi Coff. Galpare[?] Crugi, Sebastiane Dopenstene: Trib. pl. Iacobe Rudine Bonaventura Abrune, vosque senatores uniuersi vestrę liberalitatis partes esse statuetis liberalia studia liberaliter alere ac tueri. Academia Basilienfis filia vestra est, quo nomine & Galliæ reges academiam Parisiensem primogenitam filiam nominat: academia(inquam) Basilienfis filia vestra est, cui perspicitis virginem é formosissimis virginibus vestris nullam ulla venustatis indole gratiave comparabilem esse: Per-ficite igitur ut cultum ornatumque vestra amplitudine dignum consequatur. Beatum Rhenanum tot virtutum encomiis abunde academia ipsa pro sua parte refutavit, clarissimisque testimoniis docuit nulla unquam in terris academiam tam exiguo tempore tot tamque variarum laudum floribus nituisse: vos eundem Rhenanum lo-cupletiorum stipendiorum largitate pro vestra parte re-futate, ut si Beatus Rhenanus revivisset, retexat oratio-nem suam, prædicetque academiam Basiliensem magis ac magis florere, quia stipediorum proventus peramplos & permagnos habeat. Vos igitur, vos (inquam) Henrice Petree,
units.tr: As that most excellent man sang of the most excellent physician, he left Hippocrates, Galen and Aegineta as witnesses of his industry. Osvald Ber[?] also handled the hidden mysteries of theology. The works of Albanus Torinus, of Aegineta, Philaretus, Theophilus, Polybius, Epiphanius, Agapetus, Damascene, Chrysolorus, Apicius, Trallian and Philotheus, translated or illustrated, will commend his vigils forever. John Huber and Isaac Collarius, the magnificent rector of the academy, maintain and uphold the ordinary professorship with the greatest learning and equal diligence. But I, forgetful and unmindful of such wonderful talents, have not recalled them enough. The Basel academy had as professor of medicine in the German tongue Theophrastus Paracelsus, who penetrated so deeply into the inmost viscera of nature, and explored and saw through the powers and faculties of metals and plants with such incredible sharpness of wit, for the treatment of all diseases, even desperate ones, and those held by human opinion to be incurable, that medicine seems to have been born and perfected with Theophrastus. Asclepiades had such fame at Rome among a people devoted to military pursuits that he abolished all the old medicine and founded a new sect, by which all diseases were cured, often by wine, at other times by abstinence from food and wine, by rubbing the body, walking, and being carried about. And so, when kings' envoys, roused by that reputation, had offered him bribes and he had scorned them, and had restored to life a man carried from his funeral, he turned almost the whole human race to himself. Theophrastus was indeed this German Asclepiades, whom Adam Abodestinus revives at Basel, as do many other excellent physicians throughout Germany. Jurisprudence follows medicine, very famous for the fame and dignity of its illustrious jurists. For Claudius Cantiuncula taught by examples that dialectic is necessary for jurisprudence, illustrated certain books of Justinian, described the office of the judge, and joined jurisprudence with the gospel. Huldrych Iselin, Martin Huber, son of John, and Gaspar Hervagius flourished in the same chair. Marcus Hoperus, likewise captivated by the study of sacred letters, is better known for his translations of Eusebius and other sacred works. John Huldrych Zasius, son of that great Zasius, whom Basel had as professor of jurisprudence, counts it a matter of great praise that he was his teacher, and he rejoices that he was made chancellor of the emperor. John Sichard illustrated the Justinian code, and by edition and prefaces commended many authors whom he had dug out of various libraries by the emperor's command and authority. Nicholas Brieffer taught civil law with great distinction, but excelled especially in history. Basil Amerbach, Adam Petri and Samuel Grynaeus, who entered the same chair, promise things consonant with the lineage of their ancestors; but Amerbach's courteous patronage has been mentioned already, and I must embrace his humanity with particular esteem, for he wished his library, furnished and adorned with every kind of excellent book, to be open and displayed to us as often as we liked. And yet, though you may have admired a library adorned with so many books, if the owner opens himself to you fully (for modesty conceals great merits of mind, as it were), you will find him more adorned with reading and learning than his books. Samuel has nobly begun his father's likeness, and I trust greatly that he will also enlarge the heritage of praise. But you, most distinguished senator Bernard Brand, why should I pass over you in this study of praise? When the course of your honours spent your age in these studies, the Basel academy had you as a noble professor of jurisprudence; and had not the greater glory of military affairs and the fuller and more splendid administration of the state drawn you away, you would without doubt now be a most noble jurist. Your great revision of Azo, illustrated with scholia, will bear witness to this. As for history, what you can do: your chronicle of the world from its founding, written in German, will bear rich and notable testimony forever. And so, as Basel is glorious under your excellent and most prudent father, Theodore Brand, as consul, so he designates and prepares his son, who was consul years ago, not by silent votes so much as by prayers. Thus the jurisprudence of Basel has had such famous and illustrious professors until now. What of the profession of theology, what kind was it or what sort of thing was it? Theology is indeed the highest of the ordinary professions in rank, and so it is most ample in divine praises. There are two ordinary professors of the kind of profession especially praised and desired by me. Here Simon Sulzer and Huldrych Koch were heard and listened to by us constantly: for I had no greater consolation in the miseries of these civil storms than to attend their regular lectures, while the one interpreted the Old Testament in Hebrew and the other the New in Greek. For then I seemed to myself to have obtained my wish, for which the proem of the Paris academy would have been almost a capital offence to us, when I wished that our theologians would draw the purer theology of the Word of God from its own sources in such a way, and show their students how it should be drawn. Wissenburg was adorned earlier with praise in mathematics, but he is to be adorned with greater praise in theology, for he, to explain the Roman religion to the people, published the Mass in German; then with a steadfast and brave spirit he first announced the gospel at Basel, and afterwards defended it for ever. Ubelhardus delights intensely in mathematics too, but especially in the physical sciences and those suited to life, and with equal constancy he upholds the religion of his fatherland. But why do we look rather at the present courses of men from whom better things may be hoped, than recall the completed stages of those who have died? For Paul Constantine of Phrygia in this very theological course stood out above all, with published commentaries on Exodus, Leviticus and Micah, and was highly ennobled by historical study, having published a chronology embracing the whole succession of kings from the beginning of the world. I do not repeat the earlier celebrated profession of Grynaeus the father, but I maintain that his theological work especially deserves celebration. For the homilies of Chrysostom translated into Latin, the commentaries on Paul, the book on the Lord's Supper, but above all the integrity and innocence of a truly theological life, which accompanied and joined such brilliant studies, made him an outstanding theologian. Andreas Karlstadt took up a certain boasting about illustrating the Lord's Supper; but I do not think I should pass over his dispute with Grynaeus in the senate, which was by far the most welcome to the academy. Grynaeus held that stoic and perhaps truer opinion, that licentiates, masterships, doctorates and similar degrees in the universities are empty and sophistical names of learning, which are often assigned to the unworthy for a price rather than given to any learned and erudite man for the true praise of virtue, free of charge; and so Grynaeus said: "Let him who can teach, teach, and where virtue is, let it appear there." Karlstadt argued on the contrary that examinations are the tests of talents and the grades of studies, by which it could be surely proved how much progress and advancement each had made in the liberal studies, and he had the customs of the universities as the supporters of his cause, that is, very eloquent and popular patrons and orators. And so he prevailed, so that the badges of virtue, like the ornaments of the body, should be sought from their makers, as it were. Martin Borrhaus, who was esteemed among the first theologians for his philosophical and mathematical labours, but especially for his theological vigils and his professorship. What of Oswald Myconius, how great learning and how great holiness of life adorned him? He illustrated the Helvetian history of young Glarean, handed down the life and death of Huldrych Zwingli to memory, and expounded the Gospel of Saint Mark and Psalm 16 learnedly and piously. He commended several sacred works of Oecolampadius in prefaces, and made his Latin catechism; he wrote very many other things too. Indeed John Oecolampadius most easily obtains the first and chief share of this praise, so equipped and adorned with Latin, Greek and Hebrew letters that his whole life seems to have been spent on this study alone. And yet, from the Greek, especially Chrysostom, Nazianzen, Nicephorus, Theophylact and many others, translated into Latin and German, so many, so varied and so manifold are the labours and vigils, commentaries on the oracles of the Prophets and Apostles, and so many and great controversies, and so many sermons published, that the life of the most diligent reader would seem too short to read through such varied writings. And yet we judge these labours, so Herculean, to be only a small part of his wonderful talent. Against the errors of religion (which at that time had grown old in this city as in the other cities of Europe), one had to keep watch, stand firm, fight in the battle line day and night, not only with hand and tongue, but above all with a holy and uncorrupted life. And I say this not of anything common or shared with many. For in the other theologians of our age and memory, however excellent, some heat and ardour sometimes stirred up something more vehement, which even pleased them less when things had calmed down. But Oecolampadius's constancy and his equanimity, like himself, remained unchanged forever. The greatest and most serious dispute of all was about the Lord's Supper; to bring it to the truth, after the death of Oecolampadius, the Basel Confession, published in German by command of the senate, lest any hypocrite should pervert it, sanctioned and approved. And certainly to the last day of his life he disputed with that other hero of the Tigurine people of Helvetia against so grave an error, so that he left his own Sparta pure and clean, with no stain of corruption of religion. Therefore, men of Basel, God has raised up this prophet for you, through whom he might lead you to the knowledge of his gospel; keep his teaching in grateful and pious memory, preserve it deeply planted and impressed in your minds, and study diligently lest the greatest and most excellent of all goods be snatched from you. Your annals tell how great was the constancy of the Basilians in defence of Ludwig of Bavaria against the terrifying thunderbolts of the Roman pontiff, so that they threw the herald of dire curses from the Marian rock into the Rhine; and in recent and lively memory, James Meyer, consul of Basel, was a shield and spear to Oecolampadius in asserting the liberty of the gospel. You have Meyers constant and brave in preserving and keeping it; hold them in my prayers forever. Indeed, when I was passing by the dance of death in the Dominican walk and feasting my eyes on the excellent craftsmanship of the painter, I rejoiced greatly that Oecolampadius was so elegantly portrayed by your command as the teacher of all mortals in dying well; for I believe you looked at such a monument with this in mind, that not only the learned, but children, women, porters and oarsmen, and any unlettered common people, admonished by that picture, might remember that this man was the author of Christian liberty for your citizens, and that the domestic lamp of purer religion shone upon the Basilians. O shepherd, blessed with a flock so mindful and so generous! Or rather, O flock, truly blessed with a shepherd so excellent and so singular! But I cannot be torn away from that divine spirit of Oecolampadius, and thinking more intensely about him I have almost passed over John Brandmüller; yet if the genuine successor of Oecolampadian sincerity is sought in his time, I scarcely augur any more German than he for the Basilians. And so, Brandmüller, our augury is that you have begun, with outstanding virtue, to confirm doctrine and life. Therefore, men of Basel, recognise that your academy is a kind of perennial fountain of such dignity; and those who have been captivated by its society and sweetness, and also countless princes of every learning who have held no ordinary professorship, will celebrate Basel with everlasting praise. Caelius Horatius Curio, son of Caelius, who at fifteen years of age, by his published works on the greatness of divine mercy and several books of declamations in this city, aroused great expectation of himself, but death snatched him away in the course of great things. His sister Angela, besides the other adornments of a virgin, spoke not only German, Italian and French but also Latin, as her manuscript letters show, and I add her to her father's distinguished praises. John Herold, who translated histories of various peoples, some orations into Latin, but more from the Greek, Latin and Italian into German. William Gratarol, a physician, who wrote not only medical but also theological works. John Gast, who has found an excellent name for his histories, poems, parables of Augustine and Jerome, gathered like flowers, but especially for the works of Oecolampadius sought out and arranged. Conrad Lycosthenes: what industry did he not bring forth on the origins of the fatherland, on Roman antiquity, on histories, on parables of infinite kinds, apophthegms, sayings and deeds? Which of you has forgotten that Boniface Amerbach was an Apollo of Roman law, not only at Basel but throughout Germany, and that in his son Basil Amerbach he perpetuated the glory of his country as by hereditary succession? John Cono, a singular master of the Greek language; Beatus Rhenanus; John Lasco; Sebastian Tiziano; John Reuchlin; Wolfgang Capito; Conrad Gesner; Urban Rhegius; Sigismund Gelenius; Jerome Wolf; John Brenz; Conrad Pellican; and above all that immortal glory of Helvetia, Huldrych Zwingli, were the fame and glory of our academy once, and of our age. But who would think that Erasmus, who was for so many years rather a guest of the Basel academy than its perpetual dignity? But among the guests of the Basel academy John Calvin must especially be mentioned, the light of France, the light of the Christian church throughout the world, a light seen especially in this very lodging in which I am meditating and writing these things; for here, as Catherine Petit, a most select matron, singular in sanctity and wonderfully captivated by the talent of her mind, often and pleasantly told me, while she was hostess not only to Calvin but also to Ramus, the first torches of so great a light were kindled; here those illustrious and heavenly vigils of Christian instruction were written and elaborated. But Calvin will himself proclaim his glory better than anyone else, and will need no other herald. Come now, guests of the Basel academy, and our familiar friends too, succeed into this fellowship of grace and thanksgiving; for unless I add to them Andreas Pena, Peter Castelnau, Peter Pithou, John Bohin, Cornelius Bomberg, Cassiodorus Reina, Francis Beth and Sylvester Teglio, I should be thought unmindful of our learned familiarity and of our philosophical companionship in daily conversation, and ungrateful. The province looks upon Pena and Castelnau as the ornaments of its senate. Pithou as a jurist will be commended by jurisprudence itself, and by a certain especial love of history, by a great history of praises. Bohin makes himself most gratifying, not only as a physician wholesome to the Basilians, but for a certain popular kindness and grace. Cornelius Bomberg, endowed with good letters and arts and no less with a good and brave spirit, would maintain that paternal and domestic honour of publishing and making public good letters and arts, unless the times, hostile to virtues, strongly opposed him then. Cassiodorus Reina the Spaniard, though he may wish to be silent and unknown, will by no means allow himself to remain silent and unknown, given his immense labour and boundless love of his fatherland, in instructing it in sacred studies and vindicating it from impious superstition and cruelty. Almost no Italy could have produced two Italians more candid and more devoted to true piety than Francis Beth and Sylvester Teglio. Beth initiates his fatherland in the sacred things of the most Christian faith in its own language. Teglio made Machiavelli's Prince speak Latin, and daily he undertakes greater monuments of his name. And you, Marc Perez, though given the citizenship of Basel, are either the chief guest of the academy or certainly its citizen: by what proofs of praise shall I address you? For to abound in great wealth, to carry on very ample trade with all the nations of the Christian world, to know Flemish, German, Italian, Spanish and French, indeed to have cultivated the liberal arts elegantly and in good Latin, to have read through the sacred letters above all, and to have chosen the most correct of the widely differing judgements of theologians in our age: these are great and rare praises of your talent and industry. But to help your friends and fellow citizens with your wealth, to benefit nations by trade in many goods, to share with learned and unlearned peoples so differing a common language in writing and in speech, to seek from the understanding of religion not the ornament of speech but the cultivation of a better life, to support, counsel, labour for, pay for, exhort, even at the risk of salvation and life, to instruct, defend, sustain, console and champion the afflicted members of the Christian church, and to place in that your highest good, and finally to refer the instruments of virtue to the use of virtue: this is at last your solid and constant glory. And so, among countless cities, you have rightly loved above all the city most hospitable of all, in which you have shown yourself a common host of beneficence and liberality to countless mortals. Yet, if there is any limit to the praises of our academy, we cannot pass over the typography born and educated in this academy, the mother and, as it were, the nurse of so many and so excellent talents, which is the nourishment of very many citizens and the most certain source of their wealth. From here Amerbach, Froben, Episcopius, Petri, the Curios, Hervagius, Isingrin, Cratander, Oporinus, Bebel, Guarinus, Brylinger, Perna and the other noble printers have adorned Basel not only with wealth but with the fame of liberal industry among all nations. O Basel, renowned not only for the other advantages of the city and the virtues of its citizens, but for the single names of so many kinds of praise of its academy! Beatus Rhenanus wrote, men of Basel, that the Basel academy flourishes less because the income from its stipends is very slight and very small. Indeed that slightness and smallness could weigh down with its weight the palms of generous minds, but it could not oppress them so that they succumbed. And yet, excellent consuls Caspar Kruge and Sebastian Tobbenstein, tribune of the people James Rudin, Bonaventure Abrunn, and you, all senators, will decide that it is your part of liberality to nourish and protect liberal studies liberally. The Basel academy is your daughter; by this name the kings of France also call the Paris academy their firstborn daughter: the academy, I say, is your daughter, and you see that among your most beautiful maidens she is comparable to none in the disposition or grace of her beauty. Therefore see to it that she obtains the cultivation and adornment worthy of your greatness. The academy itself has amply repaid Beatus Rhenanus with many encomiums of virtue, and has shown by the clearest testimonies that never on earth did an academy shine in so short a time with so many and so varied flowers of praise; you, for your part, repay the same Rhenanus with a more generous largesse of stipends, so that if Beatus Rhenanus were to come back to life, he would retract his speech and proclaim that the Basel academy flourishes more and more, because it has very ample and very great income from its stipends. Therefore you, yes you, I say, Henry Petri,

units.la: Petrec, Ioannes Mejere, Bernarde Brande senatores eximii, academiæ patroni, patrocinium istud apud senatum suscipite. Huc frid. Menzingere qui tabulario vrbis præses, huc Luca Gerbarde, Vernere Volsine, cuius proavus in medicorum collegio primus decanus fuit, vos denique senatores universi ad hanc opem socii & adjutores accedite. Restituistis academiæ sampetreos canonicatus, monachatus, de tam multis vocantibus aliquos adjungite, ut sicuti Æneæ Sylvio gloriosum est prima tam nobilis academiæ fundamenta posuisse, ita vobis laudabile sit auxisse & exornasse. Quapropter (viri Basilienses) P. Ramus discedens jucundi, liberalis, humani hospitii memor grati animi monimentum apud vos esse εὐφημίαν istam voluit, á Deo opt.max.precatus, ut Basilea in perpetuum opibus firma, copiis locuples, gloria ampla virtute honesta, pietate præcipue insignis, religioneque sancta ac beata sit.
units.tr: Peter Petri, Johannes Meyer and Bernhard Brand, distinguished senators and patrons of the university, take up this patronage before the Senate. Hither also come Friedrich Menzinger, president of the city archive, Lukas Gerbard, and Werner Volsinus, whose great-grandfather was the first dean of the college of physicians. Finally, all you senators, join this cause as allies and helpers. You have restored the canonries and monasteries of St Peter's; add some of the many who are called to them, so that, just as it is glorious for Aeneas Sylvius to have laid the first foundations of so noble a university, it may be praiseworthy for you to have enlarged and adorned it. Therefore, men of Basel, Peter Ramus, on leaving, mindful of your pleasant, generous and kindly hospitality, wished this word of good omen [εὐφημία] to stand among you as a monument of his grateful spirit, praying to God, the Best and Greatest, that Basel may be forever strong in resources, rich in means, great in renown, honourable in virtue, especially distinguished in piety, and holy and blessed in religion.
